Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Psalm 69, drawn from the sites I could access.

---

## Psalm 69 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Title and Setting

**“To the choirmaster. To the tune of ‘Lilies.’ Of David.”** The Hebrew *Shoshannim* means “Lilies.” It may refer to the tune, a six-stringed instrument, or the beauty of the composition. Spurgeon calls this “the lily among thorns, the lily of the valley, blooming in the garden of Gethsemane.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php) Gill notes that the Targum and several rabbis interpret the psalm as concerning Israel’s captivity, but he argues it speaks of a single suffering person — the Messiah — as proven by the numerous NT citations. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm) Ellicott, however, argues the traditional ascription to David cannot fit verses 10–12 and v. 20; he regards the author as an unknown sufferer from religious persecution, with the conclusion possibly a later liturgical addition. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/69.htm)

---

### vv. 1–3: Drowning in a Flood of Trouble

**v. 1 — “Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck.”** David felt as though he was drowning. David Guzik notes this is the second Psalm beginning “Save me, O God” (after Ps 54) and draws a parallel to Peter’s cry “Lord, save me!” (Matt 14:30). Spiritually, the waters picture Jesus sinking into the deep mire of humanity’s sin and guilt. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/) Spurgeon writes: “Sorrows, deep, abounding, deadly, had penetrated his inner nature… All the sea outside a vessel is less to be feared than that which finds its way into the hold.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php) Gill applies it entirely to Christ: the waters represent floods of ungodly men, the assembly of the wicked, the curses of the law, and the wrath of God entering His very soul. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm)

**v. 2 — “I have sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing.”** Guzik contrasts this with Ps 40:2 where David rejoiced at being set upon a rock. Here he is in the opposite position — sinking in mud with no foothold. Spurgeon identifies four kinds of deep mire believers may sink into: unbelief, trial and difficulty, inward corruption, and the devil’s temptation. For Jesus, sin itself was the mire — foul and foreign to His holy nature. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/) Gill connects this to Psalm 40:2 and sees Christ bearing the filthy sins of His people, getting into “the horrible pit, the mire and clay.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm)

**v. 3 — “I am weary from my crying; my throat is parched. My eyes fail, looking for my God.”** David was worn out from praying. Spurgeon: “We are, it is to be feared, more likely to be hoarse with talking frivolities to men than by pleading with God.” Jesus’ prayers were “salted with fire, hot with agony.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php) Gill notes that Jesus’ failing eyes were one of the curses of the law (Lev 26:16), showing how in everything Christ was made a curse for His people. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm) Ligonier’s Godfrey: “His misery is highlighted by the irony that although he is drowning, he is thirsty.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/can-christians-pray-imprecations-psalm-69)

---

### v. 4: Hated Without Cause

**v. 4 — “Those who hate me without cause outnumber the hairs of my head.”** Jesus quoted this verse in John 15:25 the night before His crucifixion: “They hated Me without a cause.” Guzik: “It’s hard for us to believe that such a wonderful, godly man as David would be so hated. This is human nature, and was even more evident in the hatred without cause directed to Jesus Christ.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/) Spurgeon: “Surprising sin that men should hate the altogether lovely one… from his cradle to his cross, beginning with Herod and not ending with Judas, he had foes without number.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php)

**“Though I did not steal, I must repay.”** David was treated as guilty though innocent. Guzik traces a redemptive pattern: the devil tried to take God’s honour; Adam took the forbidden fruit; Moses took an Egyptian’s life; David took Bathsheba — but Jesus refused to take what was rightfully His (Phil 2:6), yet was condemned anyway. Gill: Christ “restored that which he took not away” — He satisfied justice He never injured, fulfilled a law He never broke, and made satisfaction for sins He never committed. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm)

---

### v. 5: Confession of Sin

**v. 5 — “You know my folly, O God, and my guilt is not hidden from You.”** This verse is a point of tension between traditions. Spurgeon says plainly: “David might well say this, but not David’s Lord; unless it be understood as an appeal to God as to his freedom from the folly which men imputed to him.” He adds: “We almost shudder when we see our brethren attempting to [apply this to Christ].” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php) Guzik takes the more common conservative approach: David confessed his own sin and failings, appealing to God’s mercy. He notes we may “spiritually apply” this to Jesus in that His bearing of our sins was public and not hidden. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/) Gill interprets it Christologically: the “foolishness” was what others accused Him of, and “my sins” refers to the sins of His people imputed to Him (cf. Ps 40:12; Isa 53:11). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm)

---

### vv. 6–8: Concern for Others; Alienation

**v. 6 — “May those who hope in You not be ashamed through me.”** David was concerned not only for himself but for the effect his suffering might have on other believers — that they might be discouraged. Guzik cites Horne: “It ought to be the prayer of every Christian, especially if he be a minister of the gospel, that his sufferings in the world may not give just offence to the brethren.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/) Gill applies this to Christ praying that His disciples’ faith would not collapse when they saw Him dead and buried. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm)

**v. 7 — “For I have endured scorn for Your sake.”** The sufferer’s reproach was borne because of his loyalty to God — not for his own faults. John Piper notes: “What is at stake is that he is jealous for God’s glory, and his adversaries reproach him for it.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/pour-out-your-indignation-upon-them)

**v. 8 — “I have become a stranger to my brothers.”** Guzik notes that Jesus’ own brothers rejected Him (John 7:5; Mark 3:21). Spurgeon: “His disciples his brethren in spirit forsook him and fled; one of them sold him, and another denied him with oaths.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php)

---

### vv. 9–12: Zeal for God’s House and Its Cost

**v. 9 — “Zeal for Your house has consumed me.”** The disciples remembered this verse when Jesus drove the moneychangers from the temple (John 2:17). Spurgeon: “Some men are eaten up with lechery, others with covetousness, and a third class with pride, but the master-passion with our great leader was the glory of God.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php) Paul also quotes the second half of this verse in Romans 15:3, applying it to Christ’s self-denial. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**v. 10 — “I wept and fasted, but it brought me reproach.”** Guzik: David repented of his sins (v. 5), and then people disapproved of his repentance. Gill notes the irony: if Christ ate, He was called a glutton; if He fasted, He was called mad (Matt 11:18). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm)

**v. 11 — “I made sackcloth my clothing, and I was sport to them.”** Spurgeon says we have no evidence Jesus literally wore sackcloth, but spiritually “as one filled with grief, was always a sackcloth wearer.” Trapp adds sackcloth was “a fashion at solemn fasts among the Easterlings; as if they thought the coarsest clothing too good for them.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**v. 12 — “Those who sit at the gate mock me, and I am the song of drunkards.”** From the city leaders (“those who sit at the gate”) to the lowest (“drunkards”), all scorned him. Spurgeon: “To this day the tavern makes rare fun of the tabernacle, and the ale-bench is the seat of the scorner.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php)

---

### vv. 13–18: Prayer for Deliverance

**v. 13 — “But my prayer to You, O LORD, is for a time of favor.”** With constant disapproval from men, David turned to God. Spurgeon: “It was a time of rejection with man, but of acceptance with God. Sin ruled on earth, but grace reigned in heaven.” Gill interprets the “acceptable time” as the time of Christ’s sufferings and death — acceptable because through it God’s good will was done, justice satisfied, and redemption finished. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm)

**v. 14 — “Rescue me from the mire.”** David turns the very words of his complaint (vv. 1–2) into prayer. Spurgeon: “It is well, if, when we complain, we neither feel nor say anything which we should fear to utter before the Lord as a prayer.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php)

**vv. 15–18 — “Do not let the floods engulf me… Answer me quickly!”** Repeated urgent appeals. David appeals to God’s *hesed* (lovingkindness) and “tender mercies.” Guzik: “By presenting himself to God as His servant and in trouble, David hoped to appeal to God’s compassion.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

---

### vv. 19–21: The Plea for Compassion

**v. 19 — “You know my reproach, my shame and disgrace.”** Adam Clarke called vv. 19–20 “one of the most forcible appeals to mercy and compassion that was ever made. The language of these two verses is inimitable.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/) Spurgeon pictures Christ: “The whole lewd and loud company is now present to thine eye: Judas and his treachery; Herod and his cunning; Caiaphas and his counsel; Pilate and his vacillation.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps069.php)

**v. 20 — “Insults have broken my heart… I looked for sympathy, but there was none.”** Ellicott notes this verse “does not give a picture of David’s condition at any time, for he always found a Nathan or a Barzillai even in his darkest hour” — pointing away from Davidic authorship. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/69.htm) Gill applies it to Christ: His disciples forsook Him and fled; no one stood with Him at His trial. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/69.htm)

**v. 21 — “They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst.”** This is quoted in the NT regarding Jesus’ crucifixion. Matthew 27:34 describes the offer of gall (or wine mixed with gall), and John 19:28–29 explicitly says Jesus was given vinegar “that the Scripture might be fulfilled.” Kidner (cited by Guzik): “What David was offered in metaphor, Jesus was offered in fact.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

---

### vv. 22–28: The Imprecatory Section — Where Traditions Differ

This is the most debated section of the psalm. Seven verses of curses on enemies.

**v. 22 — “May their table become a snare.”** The “table” represents prosperity, peace, and security (Venema, cited in Spurgeon). Paul quotes vv. 22–23 in Romans 11:9–10 to describe the hardening of unbelieving Israel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**v. 23 — “May their eyes be darkened.”** Judicial blindness. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary says: “He desired that his enemies be so heavily judged that they would have neither eyes to see nor strength to do evil any more.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-69.html)

**v. 24 — “Pour out Your wrath upon them.”** The imprecations intensify.

**v. 25 — “May their place be deserted.”** Quoted twice in the NT: by Jesus over Jerusalem (Matt 23:38) and by Peter concerning Judas (Acts 1:20). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**v. 27 — “Add iniquity to their iniquity.”** Trapp: “Punish one sin with another (by giving them up to a reprobate sense), and plague them soundly for their sin.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**v. 28 — “May they be blotted out of the Book of Life.”** The most severe imprecation in the Psalter. Maclaren: “To blot names therefrom is not only to kill, but to exclude from the national community, and so from all the privileges of the people of God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

#### How Traditions Differ on the Imprecations

**Reformed (Ligonier / Godfrey):** The imprecations are not sinful personal vengeance but prophetic approval of God’s just judgment. The NT quotes the imprecations approvingly (Acts 1:20; Rom 11:9–10). Godfrey argues the “book of the living” in v. 28 refers not to the Lamb’s Book of Life (election) but the covenant-community register from Exodus 32:33 — names can be blotted from it. Christians *may* pray imprecations against intransigently unrepentant enemies, though love for enemies must come first. Paul utters one in 1 Cor 16:22: “If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/can-christians-pray-imprecations-psalm-69)

**Reformed Baptist (Piper / Desiring God):** Piper sees two prongs in the NT use: judgment (the imprecations are “not sinful personal retaliation but prophetic approval of God’s just retribution”) and suffering (Christ’s suffering either saves or hardens). For believers today, the imprecations teach us to approve God’s coming judgment but simultaneously to forgive our personal enemies — precisely *because* judgment belongs to God alone (Rom 12:19–21). “Forebear, forgive precisely because there is judgment.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/pour-out-your-indignation-upon-them)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon notes a sharp difference between David and Christ: “We note the difference between David and the Son of David in the imprecations of the one against his enemies, and the prayers of the other for them.” He does not condemn David but distinguishes the type (David) from the antitype (Christ). Kidner (Anglican, cited by Guzik): “The very juxtaposition of David cursing his tormentors and Jesus praying for His, brings out the gulf between type and antitype, and indeed between accepted attitudes among saints of the Old Testament and the New.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik / Enduring Word):** Guzik treats the imprecations as a difficult but Scripture-honouring section. He notes it is unclear whether David meant “this is what I want God to do” or “this is what I know God will do.” He draws the contrast with Jesus’ forgiveness on the cross but also cites G. Campbell Morgan: “Neither in that prayer [‘Father forgive them’], nor in any of His teachings, can we find a word of tolerance for those who do evil, knowing that it is evil.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**Methodist/Wesleyan/Holiness (Pulpit Commentary Homiletics):** The Pulpit Commentary speaks plainly: “If we are to take the language (in vers. 22–28) just as we find it… we cannot but regard it as highly culpable. There is more here than just indignation.” It says Christians should “guard against indulgence in such language. It is not for us to judge others; it is not for us to return evil for evil.” Christ taught us to love our enemies. “If we indulge in resentment, we not only hurt ourselves, but we wrong our brother.” The writer says we should imitate the psalmist’s prayer and trust in God but not his curses. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/69.htm)

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Treats the imprecations as prophetic judgment pronounced upon the enemies of David, Israel, and Christ. The curses on the “table” (v. 22) refer to the Jewish religious privileges (Passover, sacrifices) that were abrogated when they rejected Christ. The “book of the living” (v. 28) refers to “the roll of the living in Israel” — national, covenant life — not eternal election. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-69.html)

---

### vv. 29–33: Turning to Praise

**v. 29 — “But I am in pain and distress; let Your salvation protect me, O God.”** The psalm pivots from curses to confidence. Clarke: “Literally, I am laid low, and full of pain or grief. Hence the prayer, ‘Let thy salvation, O God set me on high!’” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**v. 30 — “I will praise God’s name in song and exalt Him with thanksgiving.”** Piper preached an entire sermon on this verse: “I will magnify God with thanksgiving. When we give thanks to him from our hearts, God is magnified. Gratitude glorifies God.” (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-will-magnify-god-with-thanksgiving)

**v. 31 — “This will please the LORD more than an ox.”** Sincere praise honours God more than animal sacrifice. Horne (cited by Guzik): “A bullock was in its prime for sacrifice, under the law, when it began to put forth its ‘horns and hoofs.’” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/) The Garner-Howes commentary adds that this parallels 1 Sam 15:22: obedience and praise surpass ceremonial offerings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-69.html)

**v. 32 — “The humble will see and rejoice.”** The psalmist’s deliverance would encourage other seekers of God. Pulpit Commentary: “The humble, the afflicted, will see in it the pledge of their own deliverance.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/69.htm)

**v. 33 — “For the LORD listens to the needy and does not despise His captive people.”** A truth both of faith and experience. Guzik: “The trial of the psalmist would not be wasted. He would become a lesson to others who seek God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

---

### vv. 34–36: The Triumphant Conclusion

**v. 34 — “Let heaven and earth praise Him, the seas and everything that moves in them.”** As low as the psalm began, it soars to cosmic praise. Guzik: “Heaven and earth are not big enough to give God the praise He is due.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/)

**vv. 35–36 — “For God will save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah.”** The vision expands beyond one man’s troubles to national restoration. Ellicott questions whether this conclusion is a later liturgical addition, “speaking as it does the language of past exile times.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/69.htm) Others see it as Davidic prophecy. Guzik: “The mention of the cities of Judah and no mention of broader Israel means this psalm, or this portion of the psalm, must date to either the days of the divided monarchy or of the Babylonian exile” — though he notes this is not conclusive. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-69/) The Pulpit Commentary: “True in part of Judah and Zion, but finding its highest fulfilment in Him who is the true King of men, and whose rule alone can unite Jew and Gentile, and bring joy to heaven and earth.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/69.htm)

---

## Summary of Where Traditions Differ

| Issue | View |
|-------|------|
| **Authorship** | Traditional (Gill, Spurgeon, Guzik): David. Modern critical (Ellicott): unknown exilic or post-exilic sufferer. |
| **v. 5 (confession of sin) applied to Christ?** | Gill: Yes — sins imputed. Spurgeon: No — “we almost shudder.” Guzik: David’s own sin, but Christ applied spiritually. |
| **Imprecations (vv. 22–28)** | Reformed (Ligonier): Rightly prayed against unrepentant covenant-breakers; NT quotes them approvingly. Baptist (Spurgeon): Valid but distinguished from Christ’s own prayers. Pulpit/Methodist: “Highly culpable”; Christians must not imitate. Pentecostal (Guzik): Ambiguous whether desire or prediction; cites Morgan to soften the contrast with Jesus. |
| **“Book of the Living” (v. 28)** | Reformed (Godfrey): Covenant register, not Lamb’s Book of Life — names can be blotted. Baptist (Garner-Howes): National roll of the living in Israel. |
| **vv. 35–36 (Zion and Judah)** | Traditional: Davidic prophecy of restoration. Critical (Ellicott): Later liturgical addition from exile period. |
